MINUTES OF THE AFTERNOON SESSION
FRIDAY, APRIL 30, 1937
Hart House, University of Toronto
Toronto, Canada
The Convention was called to order by President Corcoran at 2 :20 P.M.
After Roll Call the Minutes of the Morning Session were read by the
Recorder.
Motion was duly made, seconded and passed that the Minutes of the
Morning Session should be approved as read.
The Table of Vital Statistics of the Chapter Memberships was then
distributed to the delegates.
Brother Benjamin T. Burton. Chi '21, read the report of the Treasurer
of the Executive CouncU.
On motion duly made, seconded and passed, this report was accepted
and referred to the Committee on Annual Communications.
Dral Reports were then continued by the senior delegates present from
the following Chapters :
Mu Epsilon Nu
Rho Delta Delta Epsilon Phi
Omicron Theta Theta Zeta Zeta

At the conclusion of the Mu Report, President Corcoran commented
briefly on the Table of Vital Statistics, and its importance.
Following the Report of the Rho Chapter, President Corcoran sub
stantiated the statements made by the delegate from Rho, and outlined the
causes for the peculiar position of fraternities on the campus at Wisconsin.

Page Seven

RECORDS OF THE CONVENTION

Following the Omicron Report, Brother Sidney V. Smith, Epsilon '39,
on concluding his report, tendered the desire of his Chapter to be host for
the 1939 Convention.
President Corcoran referred this matter to the delegates for their con
sideration, and commended Epsilon Chapter on its high scholastic standing.
A short discussion of constructive ideas for scholarship and Chapter
finances followed.
The Report of the Committee on Unfinished Business was read. The
report included the following resolution:
That the Chapters of Psi Upsilon bend every effort to improve
the scholastic standing of their members, and in furtherance of this
purpose, it is recommended that each Chapter:
1. Give due weight to scholastic abUity in selecting new members.
2. Establish promptly, effective upper class supervision over
study hours of freshmen to the end that -adequate time be devoted
to preparation for the work of the classroom.
3. Seek to improve attendance at classes, eliminating any tend
ency to overcut.
4. Enforce nightly hours of quiet in the fraternity house, to

permit study without disturbance or interference.
5. When feasible, with faculty co-operation, check scholastic
grades periodically, attempting to influence improvement in cases
where results are unsatisfactory.
6. Encourage inter-delegation or other competition within the
Chapter in scholastic endeavor, either by:
(a) Establishing suitable prizes or rewards for the winner.
(b) Requiring the loser to stand treat at a party.
7. In appropriate cases, establish a system of house tutors,
whereby those particularly proficient in special studies assist members
having difficulty in such studies.
A general discussion of this
report foUowed. Brother Stephen G. Kent,

A general discussion followed on the subjects of : Alumni financial
delinquency, rushing, offset lithography for the Diamond, campus cliques,
responsibUity of Psi Upsilon with respect to other fraternities, and sizes
of the Chapters.
President Corcoran concluded the discussion by stating that rushing
captains henceforth would be listed, and sent to each Chapter, and that the
size of Chapters should not be
greater than fifty members for ideal chapter
life unless unusual conditions warrant it.

Appendix A
THE ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
OF THE

EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
TO THE

1937 CONVENTION OF PSI UPSILON
HELD UNDER THE AUSPICES OF THE

EXECUTIVE COUNCIL AND THE NU CHAPTER
Toronto, Ontario, Canada
April 29. 30 and May 1, 1937

This is the one hundred and fourth year of our Fraternity and to the
CouncU
delegates and alumni from our twenty-seven chapters, the Executive
extends cordial fraternal greetings.
is
One hundred and four years is a long time and such a ripe old age
existence of fine ideal. Fine
certainly splendid testimony to the continuing a

friendships among carefully chosen men, subscribing to the ideals so beauti
fully expressed in our fine and yet simple Constitution, has brought nearly
twenty thousand men to the altars of Psi UpsUon.
On April 24, 1920, Psi Upsilon established its first chapter in Canada.
The Nu Chapter has flourished and because of the readily acknowledged
vigor of its members and their fine contributions to the ideals of Psi UpsUon
friendship, it was only natural that Psi UpsUon should grant two more
charters in Canada shortly thereafter, one at McGill University in 1928
and the other at the University of British Columbia in 1935. Psi UpsUon
is grateful for these three flourishing chapters.
Our Nu Chapter and their loyal Alumni Association have made most
attractive arrangements for this Convention and we certainly feel indebted

to them for their generosity and fine spirit.
This Year's Accomplishments :
The Executive Council is pleased to report to this Convention that the
Fraternity is in splendid condition. This statement is made not in selfglorification, but based on accurate observations. It is with regret, however,
that we have all too frequently noted that some of our ancient rivals have
encountered serious difficulties in losing the position of expected prestige
which all of their chapters should maintain.
From the reports made to the Council by its members through official
visits, and from data gathered through communications received from the
universities in which our chapters are located, and from information sent

in by the various Alumni Associations, we state with full confidence
to us

that Psi Upsilon has never been in a stronger position. We would caution

our chapters to look to their laurels so that by hard work and proper
planning we may attain ever greater usefulness to the universities wherein
we have chapters, and thus bring the members of our chapters closer to

gether, and likewise bring our chapters even more closely together.
The finances of our chapters are in good condition and with only a few
exceptions the scholarship ranking of our chapters demonstrates a record
of achievement in which the chapters take genuine pride.

During the past few years, national fraternities, particularly in the
United States, have been challenged in a few institutions as to their place
and value in the higher educational system. These late years have been
years when the very existence of everything has been questioned. All too
frequently too much emphasis has been given to the need for change. The
conservative old Owl of Psi Upsilon does not sympathize with such thinking.
We do not believe that fine friendships can change nor the ideals which they
represent. Likewise our need for real friendships, if anything, is far greater
during times of stress and turmoil. Even in view of Psi Upsilon's outstand
ing position of leadership, we are part of a system and thereby jointiy
responsible to make our contributions so that the system shall neither fail
nor falter.
This challenge to fraternities became a clear cut one at Dartmouth
College about two years ago. For the purpose of meeting this, all of the
national fraternities with chapters at Dartmouth met and appointed a com
mittee to work with the college in the experimentation and solution of this
question. Brother Emmett Hay Naylor. Zeta '09. Secretary of our Execu
tive Council, served on this alumni committee of five and has made several
trips to Hanover.
It was originally believed that the plan as outlined for the so-called
revitalization of fraternities at Dartmouth, would take at least three years,
but all of the fraternities at Dartmouth have put the three-year plan into
operation during the current college year, proving the value of fraternities
not only to their members but to the institution in which they have chapters.

A report of the experimental work as done at Dartmouth, with its
excellent results, is going to all of the chapters in the colleges and univer
sities of the United States and Canada so that they may organize and
revitalize their local chapters and make them more worth whUe to the
respective institutions and to their local membership.
There is question but that the national fraternities at Dartmouth
no

have met the challenge and proven their worth. Your Executive CouncU
desires to express its deep appreciation for the outstanding work of Brother
Naylor in this problem. It is to be hoped that ample time will be avaUable
at this Convention so that Brother Naylor may give a more detaUed report.

In this way all chapter delegates may take away with them many helpful
suggestions.

Chapter Histories :

It is expected that all chapter histories will definitely be finished by
January I, 1938. Only about one half of the chapters have completed their
histories to date. Very recently we have discovered that two or three of
the chapters have not even started on their histories. It is a solemn obliga
tion for each chapter to organize its committee of alumni and undergraduates
so that a complete and
interesting history for each of our chapters is duly
compiled.
Professor Albert C. Jacobs. Phi '21, of the Columbia Law School, has
assumed the responsibility of taking all of the individual chapter histories
and compiling therefrom Volume Number 2 of Psi UpsUon's epitome. He
is the son of the editor of our original epitome.

The Diamond :

The Diamond certainly has shown a continued marked improvement
and its regular publication since its revival in 1920 has been an important
factor in keeping our alumni and undergraduates informed of many inter
esting events in the chapters and among the alumni.
The modest endowment for The Diamond is actually insufficient to
guarantee its perpetual existence. At the earliest opportunity, plans should
be made to secure such substantial contributions towards its endowment
so as to complete it.

1938 Convention :

It is the duty of this Convention to fix the meeting place for our 1938
Convention, and according to the general scheme for rotation provided for
in the Constitution the next Convention should be held with the Iota Chapter
at Kenyon College. The last convention was held there in 1910.

Petitions :

Once more, we wish to announce that there have been no petitions for
charters of chapters in Psi Upsilon. We do not feel slighted in the least.
Delta Chapter Centennial:

February 1 1, 1937, marked the beginning of the second century of the
existence of our Delta Chapter. Appropriate festivities were arranged by
the Delta at their Chapter House on February 8 and 10; the former date
marking the annual initiation and the latter date the informal smoker and
buffet attended by many alumni and undergraduates from several chapters.
The gathering on February 10 was honored by the presence of the Chan
cellor of New York University, numerous deans and members of the
faculty who, for many years, have held that chapter in high regard. On
February 11, a formal banquet was held at the Pennsylvania Hotel in
New York City.
On behalf of the chapters, the Executive Council extended the best
wishes of the Fraternity to the Delta Chapter upon the completion of one
hundred years of splendid achievement and extending the best wishes of the
Fraternity for another century of usefulness to New York University and
to Psi UpsUon.
